name: DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit)
vendor: DPDK project (Linux Foundation), created at Intel

foundation.via: A Linux Foundation project with its own governing board and technical board

summary: C libraries and drivers for processing packets in user space at line rate: applications take NICs away from the kernel and poll them from dedicated CPU cores, with no interrupts or system calls per packet.
intro: In a normal Linux server, each packet raises an interrupt, passes through the kernel’s network stack and is copied to the application through a system call. At tens of millions of packets per second that overhead is too much. DPDK moves packet processing into the application instead. A NIC is unbound from its kernel driver and bound to `vfio-pci`, and a poll mode driver (PMD) in user space reads and writes the NIC’s descriptor rings directly. Application threads are pinned to dedicated cores and poll in a loop, so they never sleep or wait for an interrupt; packets live in buffers (mbufs) allocated at start-up from memory pools in hugepages, and cores hand work to each other through lockless rings. The Environment Abstraction Layer (EAL) hides the platform: it sets up memory, cores and PCI access on Linux, FreeBSD or Windows, on x86, Arm and POWER CPUs.

DPDK is a toolkit, not a product. On top of the core it provides drivers for NICs from many vendors and for virtual devices such as virtio and vhost-user, plus libraries and drivers for crypto, compression, event scheduling and other accelerators, and helpers for hashing, longest-prefix-match lookups, flow classification and QoS. Applications are written either run-to-completion, where each core handles a packet from start to finish, or as a pipeline of stages on different cores linked by rings. Tools such as `dpdk-testpmd` forward traffic between ports to test NICs and measure throughput.

It is the fast path inside many network functions: routers, firewalls, load balancers, wireless and wireline infrastructure, Open vSwitch’s user-space datapath, and one of the targets of the P4 compiler. Intel created DPDK in 2010, 6WIND started the open community at dpdk.org in 2013, and it moved to the Linux Foundation in April 2017. Releases are numbered by year and month and come about every four months: 26.07 came out in July 2026 and 26.11 is due on 18 November 2026. Every November release is a long-term support release, maintained for three years.
strengths: Line-rate packet processing on standard servers by avoiding interrupts, system calls and copies per packet
Broad hardware support: PMDs for NICs from many vendors plus virtio, vhost-user and accelerator drivers behind common APIs
Portable across x86, Arm and POWER, and across Linux, FreeBSD and Windows, through the EAL
A permissive BSD licence and a vendor-neutral Linux Foundation project, so it is easy to build into commercial products
limits: Polling burns whole CPU cores at 100% even when traffic is light, unless the application adds interrupt or power-saving modes
Bypassing the kernel means losing its network stack and tools: no sockets, `iptables` or `tcpdump` on those ports unless the application provides them
Setup is demanding: hugepages, binding NICs to `vfio-pci` (often with an IOMMU), core isolation and NUMA placement all have to be right
A low-level C toolkit with releases about every four months; most teams build on the November LTS and on a framework that uses DPDK rather than on DPDK directly

story: Intel created DPDK in 2010 as a set of libraries for fast packet processing on its general-purpose CPUs, and released it under a permissive licence. In 2013 6WIND established an open community around it at dpdk.org, and other CPU and NIC vendors began adding drivers.

As routers, firewalls, load balancers and other network functions moved from dedicated boxes to software on servers, DPDK became a common building block for them. On 3 April 2017 the community moved to the Linux Foundation, with a governing board of member companies, among them ARM, AT&T, Cavium, Intel, Mellanox, NXP, Red Hat and ZTE, alongside the technical board that already steered development.

The project kept its year-and-month releases and its long-term support for each November release. In 2026 it shipped 26.03 and 26.07, with 26.11, the next LTS, due in November; Open vSwitch 4.0 was validated with DPDK 25.11.

choices.why: At high packet rates an interrupt per packet, or even per batch, costs more than spinning on a dedicated core, so DPDK gives cores to the data plane and keeps them busy.
Running the NIC driver inside the application removes system calls and copies between kernel and user memory, and lets the application batch and prefetch as it likes.
Allocating all packet buffers up front in large pages avoids allocation on the fast path and reduces TLB misses when touching many buffers.
